# What are you actually choosing together?
A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.
“We’re together” can hide a lot. I might hear exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, and a whole future, while she hears, “We really like each other and we’ll see.” I don’t mind letting some things develop without naming them. I mind finding out later that one of us thought the label had already settled them.
Maybe what two people actually want is mostly practical: share a home, raise children, support each other, take care of each other, and maybe have sex. That’s common, especially outside the modern West. If both people know what they’re doing, I don’t think there’s anything inherently wrong with it. It would feel wrong to me because I want to be in love. I’d also be thinking about what happens if one of us later meets somebody we really do fall for and starts wondering why we settled.
What I want is romance without pretending I can promise a future emotion. Two people can really be in love and choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life together. I still can’t know exactly what my heart will feel ten years from now.
So before I commit, I want to know what we think we’re actually joining and what we’re really promising. If the romance changes, which parts are supposed to remain? What happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? Is that itself betrayal, or does betrayal mean lying or breaking an agreement? Which needs are we expecting to keep outside the relationship? When do we revisit the agreement? If we separate, what do we still owe each other and any children?
My actual ideal is still to have intimacy embedded in community. Most people aren’t going to move into a free-love community, so as Pema Chödrön says, “Start Where You Are.” Keep friendships and other sources of meaning and support alive while you figure out what kind of relationship you’re actually building.
